cameras are increasingly used in mobile applications due to their ability to accurately detect both near and far obstacles under various lighting conditions. Their high depth resolution, however, also leads to unwanted small textual features that must be filtered out by the vehicle's software. This paper assesses the current state-of-the-art monocular ToF sensors in terms of their depth maps' quality on mobile platforms. Two of their characteristics are investigated: range finding accuracy and noise presence. A custom-built database of recorded real-world ToF images, combined with artificially intensified noise and cleaned up images of both near and far scenes, allows for a comprehensive evaluation of these sensors. Three experimental setups are conducted on a mobile device: (1) comparing the effectiveness of four available software approaches in eliminating noise from both near and far scene images; (2) comparing the performance of two NVIDIA hardware-based denoising methods in eliminating noise from both near and far scene images; and (3) evaluating the range finding accuracy of both Intel and Sony hardware in both near and far scene images. This evaluation reveals that a specific NVIDIA hardware-based denoising method exhibits significantly lower noise variance than both Intel-based ToF and its own denoising algorithm, resulting in nearly noise-free images. Additionally, it has been found that smaller depth map noise results in more accurate range finding accuracy. This outcome motivates the development of new hardware and algorithms aimed specifically at reducing noise in low-contrast ToF images. By doing so, it is possible to further improve the range finding accuracy of both Intel and Sony ToF sensors. A database of natural video footage that incorporates significant amounts of both near and far scene images, resulting in reduced range finding accuracy in these areas, is also contributed to the public domain. This database can serve as a natural evaluation benchmark for any new hardware or algorithms designed to improve the overall quality of ToF images, particularly in mobile applications, by accurately modeling real-world scenarios and depth maps. A subsequent study builds upon these findings by demonstrating the significant impact of incorporating noise-reduced ToF images on mobile application usability. To address this problem, two new algorithms for both hardware and software are proposed in this study. Experimental results indicate that these algorithms are effective in further enhancing the depth maps' quality of both Intel and Sony ToF sensors in real-time. Furthermore, it has been found that using these noise-reduced ToF images results in notable performance improvements of up to 25.7% and 18.1% in pedestrian detection and semantic segmentation tasks, respectively. Specifically, we modify the Heisenberg quantum lattice model for our purposes, considering the effect of quantum fluctuations using two different methods. One method utilizes a perturbative approach based on a local mean-field solution, while the other employs a nonperturbative approach using a matrix product state to incorporate quantum fluctuations in a effective two-body Hamiltonian. Both methods yield similar results and show a clear nonlocal response observed in our experiments, which is evident in two scenarios: when reducing the energy gap between the two-well and single-well confining potentials, and when increasing the strength of the inter-species interaction between the two gases. The ability of our effective Hamiltonian to describe the experiment accurately supports its validity and suggests potential applications in manipulating separate components of a superposition of optical lattices using a probe atom to assess the local properties of another, target system. Furthermore, incorporating a weak connection between the two-well confining potential and the presence of a local impurity in one of the wells allows us to study the effect on the nonlocal response, which presents an extension of the nonlocal response phenomenon discovered in our previous work. Finally, by analyzing the long-term behavior of the system and using a constrained mean-field approach, we reveal that the nonlocal response exhibits a signature of quantum correlation that emerges when both systems have bosonic properties, which differs when one system contains fermionic properties due to the presence of inter-species tunneling. Hence, this finding offers an alternative method for producing entangled states without the need for direct coupling between the two gases, which poses as a potential mechanism to create bi-linear supersolid states. Lastly, we propose an experiment involving the application of separate magnetic gradients to individual wells in order to study the nonlocal response under a variety of conditions without compromising the purity of the individual Bose-Einstein condensates. Furthermore, we propose an extension of this experiment with the incorporation of separate gravitational gradients in conjunction with locally applied spin-orbit coupling, which enables mapping the nonlocal response onto the parameter space and exploring different quantum many-body phenomena such as nonlocal response, supersolid formation and emergent bi-linear bond order. Ultimately, this research offers a range of possibilities to manipulate and study quantum many-body systems via nonlocal response as a future perspective for atom interferometry and quantum information processing. The advancement of computational capabilities has led to the development of more sophisticated software programs that can accurately calculate settings for protective devices using measurement data. Despite the effectiveness of these methods, questions regarding uncertainty remain, as measurements contain errors and an acceptable limit on system instability is required. This research outlines a new approach for designing protective device timing using the time-domain phasor approach. This method is comparable to existing instantaneous-based distance methods in that it uses instantaneous voltage and current values to calculate device timing; however, it considers secondary arm variation by employing instantaneous voltage and current phasors, which are then translated into a time-domain response through the use of an equivalent T-φ domain transfer function. This method has the advantage of accounting for the duration of transient events and is influenced by the degree of secondary variation. The research demonstrates this new approach by using actual waveform data from a modern distribution feeder to calibrate a nonlinear load model for both residential and commercial properties. The study relies on measurement uncertainty and applies it to the time-domain phasor model for fault analysis on the distribution system to establish a tolerance zone for protective device timing. The proposed method for protective device timing with uncertainty considerations matches the specifications of existing instantaneous-based distance algorithms in terms of fault sensitivity and performance. Furthermore, by utilizing measurements from actual distribution feeders and considering the degree of secondary variation, protective device timing with uncertainty has been validated. Additionally, under diverse fault conditions, it has been demonstrated that this new approach for protective device timing can reduce operating currents compared to existing instantaneous-based distance algorithms. Lastly, protective device timing with uncertainty has been shown to be compatible with various fault configurations. The advancement of computational capabilities has led to the development of more sophisticated software programs that can accurately calculate settings for protective devices using measurement data. Despite the effectiveness of these methods, questions regarding uncertainty remain, as measurements contain errors and an acceptable limit on system instability is required. This research outlines a new approach for designing protective device timing using the time-domain phasor approach. This method is comparable to existing instantaneous-based distance methods in that it uses instantaneous voltage and current values to calculate device timing; however, it considers secondary arm variation by employing instantaneous voltage and current phasors, which are then translated into a time-domain response

Current plagiarism detection tools designed for academic papers face difficulties when processing social media content, largely because they were developed with a different focus. This research aims to create a novel approach utilizing deep learning for social media plagiarism detection, where tokenization and representation learning processes are optimized to accommodate the unique characteristics of cross-language and cross-format data. When compared with existing state-of-the-art plagiarism detection methods, our approach achieves better results on two distinct social media datasets one comprising Hindi and English, and the other consisting of German and English, both sourced from Twitter and Facebook. Notably, our model's accuracy is 85.80% for the Twitter dataset containing mixed Hindi and English content, 84.02% for the Facebook dataset containing mixed Hindi and English content, 80.99% for the Twitter dataset containing mixed German and English content, and 80.50% for the Facebook dataset containing mixed German and English content. This performance compares positively with the GreenLeaf tool that was utilized as a benchmark and achieved results of 80.36%, 79.48%, 69.90%, and 74.81% for the four mentioned datasets. Each dataset was composed of 1,000 posts, and all analysis was carried out using a high-performance computing infrastructure consisting of 100 Linux-powered nodes, each equipped with 16GB RAM and 4 CPUs. Consequently, our model's output compares favorably with the GreenLeaf tool. This research successfully developed a novel deep learning-based approach for social media plagiarism detection, particularly for cross-language contexts, where analysis was conducted on two distinct datasets, one comprising mixed Hindi and English content, and the other containing mixed German and English content, both sourced from Twitter and Facebook. Our focus is on addressing the issue of post-hoc feature importance evaluation for deep neural networks with non-differentiable outputs and interconnected weights. We propose a unified framework with both local and global feature importance estimation capabilities, offering the benefits of model-agnosticity, transparent calculations, and easy implementation. Our method doesn't necessitate perturbing network architecture or training and can be used in conjunction with existing networks. Additionally, it is accompanied by theoretical bounds. We demonstrate the efficacy of our method in comparing model performances, selecting optimal features, and improving adversarial robustness. ) to solve complex, high-dimensional inverse problems where data is scarce goes to the heart of machine learning. When these problems have natural constraints - for instance, being located within a city's boundaries in a taxi's destination prediction task - we can harness this information to make predictions more accurate. Annulators, a recently proposed framework for ANNs, are capable of incorporating geometric constraints into their architecture. By incorporating classical numerical methods, Annulators can guarantee that generated outputs lie within the defined bounds. 

    This paper extends the concept of Annulators to develop a new framework for tackling multi-variable inverse problems. By integrating a linear programming algorithm like Simplex, Annulators can ensure the resulting outputs are valid. We apply this methodology to a multi-variable problem where we need to predict input data for a given output, with the constraint that the predicted input must be within the feasible region defined by a linear bound. Compared to traditional neural networks, Annulators show a superior results in terms of both accuracy and efficiency. Furthermore, we identify a limitation in existing models used for comparison and propose a modified version. After optimization, the modified model exhibits better performance with Annulators. The code used for these experiments is available at https://github.com/tiemelu/Annulators. 

    Based on these findings, there is considerable potential in developing more sophisticated models within this family, and we have presented the development of a basic version. Future research could involve extending this concept to other areas, such as taxi destination prediction, where the defined constraints can lead to more accurate and efficient ANNs. Furthermore, we may be able to improve the performance of Annulators using deeper architectures, such as with ReLU activation or a more complex LP algorithm. Additionally, there may be opportunities to develop hybrid models that integrate local models, such as GP, with global models, such as DNN, using techniques like gauging for ANNs and comparing the resulting outputs for validity. Finally, we may be able to develop hybrid models that integrate Annulators with other areas of machine learning, such as data augmentation or feature selection.

The resulting linear optimization problems can be solved using linear programming methods, but the increased memory and time requirements can become significant as the problem sizes increase. Various sparse and compact representations have been developed to mitigate these limitations, but they do not address the inherent non-convex nature of these problems, which often necessitates global optimization rather than approximate relaxation methods. Specifically, to assess public participation processes governed by law, researchers must extend the concept of impact beyond traditional, general measurements to examine their application in domestic and international contexts. This concept is crucial in the digital age, presenting opportunities to leverage big data and machine learning techniques for enhanced measurements. By building upon the existing understanding of impact as a set of general, hierarchical measurements, we refine this concept to better suit the unique challenges of public participation, and we discuss its potential future developments, including the integration of machine learning algorithms. Our results show that the proposed framework can facilitate the evaluation of public participation processes under national and international law. Ultimately, we suggest that the proposed impact assessment framework, with its hierarchical structure, offers a structured approach to incorporating the outcomes of machine learning algorithms and big data analysis within the traditional understanding of impact. Furthermore, we recognize the promising potential of this approach in the context of international human rights, given the significant advancements in machine learning algorithms in recent years. As part of our discussion, we present potential applications of machine learning algorithms in the assessment of public participation, including in the areas of global health governance and human rights. Despite the existing literature on the impact of public participation, there remains a lack of clear guidelines for its measurement. $k$-Satisfiability problem, denoted as $k$-SAT, is defined by $k$ clauses, each consisting of at most $l$ literals, where each literal is either a variable or its negation. If we modify each clause to include all possible literals, the resulting formula would be a $k$-Color-3SAT instance, a known NP-hard problem, with each variable having up to $l$ possible values. 

  A sub-$k$-Color-3SAT instance is a part of a $k$-Color-3SAT instance, with at most $rk$ variables, for some $r<1$. This paper proves that solving sub-$k$-Color-3SAT instances, for $r$ close to 1, is still an NP-complete problem, even with restricted $k$, and shows that various algorithms fail on a modified 3-SAT instance, despite it being solvable. 

  Specifically, when $r$ is close to 1, we observe the collapse of three well-known algorithms: 
  1) Davis-Patterson-Lehman, 
  2) Krom, and 
  3) Jelim. 
  These algorithms fail to use the $k$-Color-3SAT constraints to solve the instance correctly, despite being correct for 3-SAT. 
  Moreover, when the number of literals $l$ is very high and $r$ is close to 1, we prove the solvability of sub-$k$-Color-3SAT instances, revealing yet another instance where conventional solving methods fail. 
  A consequence of this failure is shown in real-world scenarios, specifically in the solution of recursive mechanical linkages and their applications in kinematics problems. 
  Hence, the conventional solving methods are insufficient for these instances and future solutions must take into consideration the binary nature of variables in the 3-SAT formula. 
  Lastly, an observation about how concave space might affect the complexity of solving $k$-Color-3SAT, in contrast to 3-SAT, is presented and discussed. 
  Furthermore, the potential for dynamic switching between discrete and continuous solving of $k$-Color-3SAT, in the case of large $l$, is explored. 
  A note on how one might achieve this using convex optimization over the dual space of variables' values, for the general 3-SAT case, is included in the appendix.

This method, based on averaging field values over many realizations of their statistical distribution, yields two key outcomes. Firstly, it reduces fluctuations in field values and, secondly, it preserves the field's time-evolution dynamics. We have identified a specific averaging procedure that effectively removes ultraviolet fluctuations, thereby allowing us to obtain an averaged and non-fluctuating field value. This, in turn, meets two essential criteria: it is invariant to any possible field configurations and also remains consistent regardless of the field's initial values. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our theoretical framework using two contrasting cases. In the first instance, we start by evaluating field autocorrelation over time in a scenario where backslash averaging is not considered and observe how field values become severely disrupted by quantum fluctuations. In stark contrast, we find, in the second case, that field autocorrelation, evaluated through averaged and fluctuation-reduced fields, behaves in a far more coherent and predictable manner. Furthermore, field values aligned with the average equilibrium density also yield a visibly extended equilibration time, measured in terms of the violation of the fluctuation-dissipation theorem. Overall, our proposed method has significant implications for any field theory dynamics model and could potentially help in determining whether a particular theory exhibits non-equilibrium dynamics similar to those seen in classical and quantum systems exhibiting disorder-driven or out-of-equilibrium phase transitions. Furthermore, this method may be particularly useful for analyzing renormalized perturbation theory in complex systems beyond classical field theories. This relation is substantiated through field binning methods as well as through an examination of the fluctuation-dissipation theorem's violations. Ultimately, this relationship highlights an intriguing phenomenon, where reduced fluctuations lead to an extended equilibration time, which in turn is most pronounced in the early stages of time evolution discussed here. This study aims to fill this gap by using a safety assessment process. Results indicated that D-alpha noise tends to synchronize with the field fluctuation caused by the magnetohydrodynamic mode in the internal wall, usually the second mode. In this synchronization, the frequency of the D-alpha emission reduces in proportion to the Mach number, suggesting that the power driving D-alpha emission stems from the ion acoustic turbulence tied to the MHD mode. Moreover, the data showed that D-alpha noise becomes less synchronized when the plasma fills the scrape-off layer more completely, indicating an increased connection between the scrape-off layer and the edge plasma mode. In addition, when the experiment involves IMF coating, the effect of the low-n, high-m mode is more pronounced than before, likely caused by the extension of the magnetohydrodynamic mode in the scrape-off layer and solenoidal field, reducing the effectiveness of the plasma edge solenoid in suppressing D-alpha emission. In both cases, the data indicate that the edge plasma mode has a greater effect on D-alpha emission than before, with implications for understanding particle and energy transport in the edge region. The findings also offer a means for directly observing the edge magnetohydrodynamic mode and its associated processes, which are difficult to study using X-ray emitters due to their limited number of emitters. Furthermore, when the plasma fills the scrape-off layer more completely, the effect of the low-n, high-m mode is less pronounced than before, which could be because the edge plasma mode no longer matches D-alpha emission as well due to the extended scrape-off layer. This standard requires small data packets to be transmitted regularly according to a device's message pattern. Similar to existing cellular technologies, 3GPP's IoT standards will use licensed spectrum but will be vulnerable to interference from unauthorised users, referred to as intruders. This paper examines the potential for illegal access in 3GPP's IoT networks and introduces a novel detection method using an adaptive linear spectral angular regression filter. This approach identifies the dominant frequencies within multi-channel data streams without prior knowledge of the number of active channels, and distinguishes normal usage from illegal activity in plots of spectral data. Experimental results show that my method can effectively detect intruders in IoT networks with an F1 score of 0.84 for short-term detection and 0.78 for long-term detection, outperforming existing graph-based methods. Moreover, successful deployment of my method requires minimal computational resources, including polynomial of time and $p$-space, as well as $p$-norm of weights, making it more efficient than previous solutions. This paper also showcases real-world case studies of illegal access in IoT networks, including a car park scenario and a smart city campaign. Overall, my method is capable of identifying illegal activity in IoT networks, characterised by sudden changes in spectral data, and can detect the presence of multiple intruders within a single data stream. A corresponding source code is available at https://github.com/Lauren-Carney/3GPP-IoT-intruder-detection. This repository includes the Jupyter notebooks used for data analysis as well as the implementation of my detection method in Python. Furthermore, an experiment was conducted using the US driving dataset from the https://archive.ks.fi/ dataset to verify the effectiveness of my method in detecting illegal activity in real-world data. Additionally, an experiment was conducted to evaluate the impact of reduced sampling rates on intruder detection, demonstrating that my method is robust even at low sampling rates. This was achieved by reducing the sampling rate to 10% of its original value while maintaining an F1 score of 0.79, and scaling down the time series data to 20% of its original size without affecting the performance of my method. Consequently, my method has been validated through successful detection of illegal activity in real-world datasets, and has demonstrated robustness in the presence of reduced sampling rates and manipulated data. These team characteristics can significantly impact work productivity on both quantitative and qualitative levels, particularly in terms of mortality rates and error frequency. Nevertheless, it is often challenging to identify the specific contributing factors when a team exhibits multiple diverse traits. This research aims to develop new statistical methods that can address this issue by creating two main models. The first is a hybrid model that integrates multiple performance metrics to identify how different team composition factors influence errors. The other is a factorial model that can quantify the distinct effects of individual diversity factors, even when teams display multiple diverse traits. Both models rely on the same conceptual framework, allowing for the identification of various team composition factors and their interaction effects. The hybrid model prioritizes the interpretation of error rate data, using the error rate as a response variable and various team composition factors as predictors. The factorial model, on the other hand, focuses on the interpretation of mortality rate data, viewing the mortality rate as a response variable and the logit-transformed mortality rate as a key factor. The combination of both models can significantly enhance the understanding of how different team composition factors contribute to error rates. The efficacy of these models was validated through the analysis of a real-world dataset, with the results indicating that both models can accurately identify significant team composition factors and their interaction effects. Understanding the accuracy of an AI model is crucial, especially when its output is subject to uncertainties due to the interpretation of natural language text. A new approach has been developed that leverages pre-trained Transformer models to model the probabilistic characteristics of inputs in AI models. By representing these uncertainties in Bayesian Networks, this method facilitates the computation of posterior probabilities, thereby enhancing the evaluation of AI models and their confidence intervals. Moreover, it can be used for posterior inference, such as selecting relevant training data to refine AI models and increase their reliability. The proposed approach has been successfully evaluated using a large-scale dataset for scenario-based reasoning. The experiment results indicate that our approach accurately captures the uncertainties in AI models and significantly improves the scalability of Bayesian model averaging for robust AI models in complex scenarios. Additionally, this model can effectively handle large datasets and is highly compatible with various AI models, such as those employing Transformers and Conditional Random Fields (CRFs), as well as those trained using multi-instance learning (MIL) for robustness. The proposed approach has been made available through an open-source implementation, including all essential tools and techniques for handling uncertainties in AI models and their applications for scenario-based reasoning. A corresponding demo can be accessed via an online tool, demonstrating this approach's capabilities. The related source code is hosted at https://github.com/HumanCentricRoboips/dynamic-kb-bayes-attention, while the model's hyperparameters are documented at https://hcrob.gitlab.io/dynamic-kb-bayes-attention. methods, Monte Carlo Inverse Problems (MCIP), offers a potential solution to the growing number of unknowns in the field of scientific modeling. MCIP utilizes deep neural networks to map Monte Carlo-generated random noise to the input parameters of a model, thereby reducing the number of necessary Monte Carlo simulations. MCIP has shown promise in applications including the inversion of satellite data and the generation of synthetic scenarios. However, the conventional formulation of MCIP poses limitations, particularly in scenarios where the model's forward operator is expensive to compute multiple times or when the desired model states exceed the capacity of a single neural network. Our study addresses these limitations by developing a novel MCIP framework that incorporates analytical gradients of the Monte Carlo method. This approach enables the optimization of neural networks in an unbiased manner and allows for the direct computation of Monte Carlo gradients using finite differences or an exact derivative. We also introduce a generalized Bayesian inversion framework for generating synthetic scenarios. Furthermore, the study demonstrates an efficient MCIP implementation for large model classes that cannot be modeled through their forward operator. In specific, the study utilizes a complex large-scale atmosphere-advection-diffusion model with 2D spatial resolution and multiple Monte Carlo simulations. The results show that our method reduces the number of necessary Monte Carlo simulations by almost 1 order of magnitude, resulting in approximately 310 simulations. This achievement is comparable to the most recent Monte Carlo Inverse Problems research with similar models. Moreover, the study demonstrates that using finite differences to compute the Monte Carlo gradient, the model can be restored with a similar level of accuracy as when using the exact derivative. Although the study's results apply to a pre-existing model, the method can be extended and utilized for any model with a defined forward operator or a implicit partial differential equation that can be solved through an iterative process. In such cases, the Monte Carlo integration can directly sample the solution of the implicit model and the Monte Carlo Inverse Problems would only rely on pre-processing and post-processing steps. This approach can integrate any numerical solver as a Monte Carlo source and allows the model to have multiple state variables, which are not feasible with traditional MCIP formulations. Finally, the study demonstrates an MCIP uncertainty interval that is significantly larger compared to conventional inversion methods with a single Monte Carlo integration, highlighting the potential for establishing robust uncertainty intervals without the need for computationally expensive Monte Carlo simulations. The novel framework and methods presented in this study aim to overcome the limitations of Monte Carlo Inverse Problems and expand the scope of deep learning and Monte Carlo methods in the field of inverse problems. In the case where $G$ is an affine symmetric Lie group and $H$ is its maximal unimodular subgroup, we show that this space is spanned by the images of harmonic forms from a specific domain $D^*(\mathbb{R}^n,G,H)$, which are derived from the Harish-Chandra c- functions. Additionally, we provide a direct, explicit description of the harmonic forms in this domain. This work has broader implications for understanding invariant harmonic forms on solvable Lie groups and their relation to the double dual Harish-Chandra transform for nilpotent Lie groups. In particular, this description can be used to derive an expression for the double dual Harish-Chandra transform in terms of elementary Harish-Chandra functions. Lastly, a similar investigation was conducted for the space of $G$-invariant invariant polynomials on $\mathbb{R}^n$. In the case where $G$ is an affine symmetric Lie group, we show that this space is spanned by the images of functions from a specific domain $P^*(\mathbb{R}^n,G,H)$. Additionally, we provide a direct, explicit description of the invariant polynomials in this domain. In the context of real affine Lie groups, the descriptions of these forms and polynomials can be specialized, resulting in the discovery of new, interesting mathematical structures, such as the computation of cohomology spaces for nilpotent Lie algebras with abelian nilradical and of the invariant polynomials for the generalized Weyl groups within the context of simple Lie algebras. In the context of complex affine Lie algebras, the descriptions of these forms and polynomials can be specialized, resulting in the computation of cohomology spaces for complex nilpotent Lie algebras with complex nilradical. Furthermore, this investigation reveals that the nilpotent Lie algebra dual to the generalized Weyl group of a simple complex Lie algebra is isomorphic to the direct sum of three subalgebras: the algebra of horizontal endomorphisms of the complex Euclidean space, the center of the algebra, and a subalgebra corresponding to the weights of a specific representation. compiler optimization that adapts the execution of programs at runtime according to varying computational environments. Although initially promising, the development of high-performance instruction tuning methods has been hindered by the high cost of creating and refining these procedures. This cost is particularly attributed to the time-consuming process of gathering performance data, which typically requires running the program on a variety of hardware systems. To alleviate this difficulty, we introduce a novel technique called PreTune, a fully automatic method for approximating the performance data of instruction tunes. Using static code analysis and an understanding of underlying CPU architectures, PreTune is able to identify likely tune candidates and assess their expected performance impacts through instruction-level simulation. The evaluation of PreTune within the context of a state-of-the-art instruction tuning system, known as HipSTT, reveals substantial promise, with the ability to decrease the time required to create and refine instruction tunes by as much as 75% without any consequent loss in performance. Furthermore, the data collected through PreTune often closely aligns with the results of actual performance measurements, underscoring its value as a complementary tool for tuning system operators. Ultimately, by integrating PreTune into the HipSTT framework, we achieve a more efficient dynamic instruction tuning system that requires less manual effort to operate effectively and is also capable of producing higher-quality tunes at a faster rate. The method and implementation details of PreTune are freely available via open-source licenses to support both research and practical applications.  The source code is shared via this link: https://github.com/quantact-ucb/PreTune, and the HipSTT system at this link: https://github.com/quantact-ucb/HipSTT. It is also publicly available through this link a set of performance measurement results for tunes identified by PreTune and HipSTT, under the supervision of Dr. Kim, the corresponding author of this work. However, the data collection results do not match the expectations at the time of analysis and needs to be re-executed and re-analyzed for accuracy and relevance. Furthermore, the analysis of the gap between the expected and actual performance under different computational conditions reveals opportunities to create even more effective instruction tunes that generalize better to a variety of systems at a faster rate. One potential direction is to create a dataset of performance measurement results for tunes identified by PreTune and HipSTT under the guidance of Dr. Kim, the corresponding author of this work, that can be used to train machine learning models that aid in dynamic instruction tuning.

We introduce a new method that allows IOA to gauge the effectiveness of novel policies without manual intervention or prior knowledge. It has a straightforward formulation as the requirement that the price of any asset must be a continuous martingale when discounted. This concept has been expanded upon by M. Jessen to include the pricing integral of an asset, which remains a martingale when discounted, under the assumption of a measurable and finite measure. We broaden the scope of No--arbitrage by relaxing the measure space constraints, allowing for general measures, finite or infinite, and non--measurable. In return, we need to impose continuousity on the price distribution functions across time. This expanded concept still yields the result that submartingales correspond to assets whose prices consistently exceed their initial value. We also prove that with certain assumptions regarding distribution functions on compact time intervals, the pricing integral can serve as a continuous martingale when discounted. Moreover, our research shows that in cases where the measure is finite with respect to time, the pricing integral can be expressed as the limit of a martingale converging to its limit as time goes to infinity. This expanded No--arbitrage theory has practical implications in theoretical financial modeling, particularly in the pricing of commodities, as illustrated using the Jessen example and a discussion on commodity pricing. Ultimately, our research demonstrates that the No--arbitrage theory is robust against modifications in the measure space and its infinite nature, which was previously thought not possible according to prior literature. Furthermore, our work bridges the gap between continuous and discrete time pricing models and offers a potential approach for generalizing the theory to discrete time frameworks. However, such generalization results in the loss of the submartingale property. As an exception to the No--arbitrage condition, we present a counterexample that demonstrates the existence of an arbitrage opportunity when the pricing integral of an asset, whose price distribution functions exhibit discontinuities, follows a path that is finite with respect to time. Additionally, our research indicates that the notion of strong No--arbitrage, which requires the absence of an arbitrage opportunity when initially positive wealth is invested, remains unattained if distribution functions are permitted to be discontinuous. However, if distribution functions are continuous, particularly when the wealth is initially invested at a zero level, the notion of strong No--arbitrage is implicit. Lastly, our research shows that the No--arbitrage condition is consistent with the up-to-the-mark model for commodity pricing, which was previously contested by Gombani et al. in their paper. method, which is a widely used technique for simulating free surface flows, can suffer from inaccuracies due to its simple volume tracking approach. The errors associated with this method tend to be more pronounced in complex flows with high surface distortions and accurate numerical solutions require small cut-off values that are difficult to choose in cases of surface instabilities. A new high-order accurate numerical scheme has been developed to model surface instabilities in free surface flows using a combination of monotonicity-preserving limiters and the exact solution to a diffusion equation. The proposed scheme is applicable to both VOF and level set methods and maintains properties such as the conservation of surface area, the free boundary condition, and the positive volume of the fluid. The method is effective in preserving monotonicity, detecting surfaces and it's validated with a range of test cases including stationary, moving and unstable free surface flows. A set of local indicators has been developed to control the gradient error using a range of monotonicity-preserving limiters and the method performs well in various test cases. The method is capable of reaching a convergence rate of at least second order accurate in smooth regions of the flow field and it can reach a rate of at least fourth order accurate in regions with known exact solutions. Furthermore, the method is capable of detecting surfaces with an accuracy of at least fifth order accurate in various test cases. A set of complex multiphase simulations including the flow over a teardrop at high speeds and the flow past a square cylinder at Reynolds numbers up to 100,000 are also performed and the method preserves the characteristic non-physical parameters of the flow with an accuracy of at least fifth order accurate. The method enables the computation of high Reynolds and Rayleigh numbers flows and the development of mass and momentum flux diagrams that match perfectly with experimental and numerical data of high-order accurate solutions in various degrees of surface instabilities. Moreover, the method enables the computation of free surface flows at a wide range of speeds, including transonic and supersonic speeds, and the free boundary condition is maintained with an accuracy of at least fifth order accurate in regions with strong gradients. The method enables the computation of complex and strong interactions between the movements of the free surface and the flow, which cannot be captured with lower-order accurate solutions in various test cases. The method enables the free surface to reach speeds of at least 260m/s and captures the physical creation of the primary vortex in the tear drop flow at a speed of 80m/s with a specific moment of inertia that matches perfectly with experimental data.

However, existing deep learning-based methods are often unreliable when processing shape-based classification tasks, often producing inconsistent outcomes for objects with minor size and positional variations. To address this limitation, our method enhances a deep learning model's robustness to size and positional changes by employing dimension-wise size normalization. This technique involves adjusting the dimension sizes of an input object to match the average dimensions of the training dataset. Unlike traditional size normalization methods that involve transforming object sizes across all dimensions simultaneously, our method calculates the size adjustments independently for each dimension, resulting in more accurate predictions. Experimental outcomes confirm that our proposed method accelerates training and achieves higher accuracy compared to conventional size normalization approaches. Notably, prediction accuracy improves significantly when applying our method to 2D and 3D shape classification tasks, achieving a recall rate of 95% for 3D classification prediction when there is up to 20% random size variation. The experimental results indicate that our method can reliably transfer knowledge across different size variation scenarios. Moreover, the extracted feature maps indicate that our method enhances model robustness to size changes by promoting the development of subtle spatial features. This is in line with our objective of enhancing model robustness to size and positional changes by incorporating domain-specific data preprocessing methods. Our method's source code is available on GitHub at https://github.com/GUOGUOQI/tree-size-normalization.

be regarded as vast-scale versions of three-dimensional number puzzles, consisting of identical spherical bodies arranged within irregularly-shaped voids. Using x-ray microcomputed tomography, researchers have noninvasively examined the internal structures of these polycrystalline solids, represented by a system of packed spheres within a larger framework of interconnected pores. Specifically, researchers have applied advanced analytical techniques, including the radial distribution function and network analysis of both the solid and void domains, as well as the study of "planar cells" in the crystal structure, to gain a more detailed understanding. Both end-to-end learning methods, which typically rely on dense feature maps, and weakly supervised ones, which do not, face challenges in ensuring geometric consistency.  While end-to-end methods can easily access dense feature maps, they tend to produce poor matches with large errors.  On the other hand, weakly supervised methods, which are restricted by inconsistent dense matching, strive to focus learning on key areas only.  Inspired by classic geometric vision methods, we introduce a unique framework that combines a supervised dense detector and an unsupervised dense matcher.  The former extracts dense matching features and generates matching scores with geometric support, while the latter only needs to focus on matching pairs with much less input data.  By incorporating geometric support into the supervision of the matcher, geometrically consistent matching is achieved, and additional supervision on matching pairs is established through geometric vision methods.   This paper explores a novel approach called data value assignment, which determines the importance of each example in the training dataset based on its contribution to model prediction accuracy. 

  This contribution is evaluated using two metrics: first, the proximity of the unlabelled data point to decision boundary classes, and second, the similarity in feature patterns between the unlabelled data and labelled data.

  An algorithm is proposed to select data points based on these contributions and an established dataset (MNIST) is used for testing the method's effectiveness compared to random sampling.

  Results show that even simple features (like pixel intensity) yield better results than random sampling. 

  Furthermore, when incorporating more complex vector transformations (like dimension reduction) the performance improvements are more substantial.

  It is anticipated that this method will enhance the accuracy of subsequent active learning methods in the field of deep learning. 

  Future work involves applying data value assignment to more complex datasets and incorporating it into semi-supervised learning. 

  Additional research is required to analyze the computational complexity of data value assignment. 

  Finally, it is important to further investigate the importance of using decision boundary classes in assigning value to data points in the unlabelled dataset.

This high-field plasma is produced by discharging a high-pressure, high-recovery gas such as xenon through a constricted nozzle into a magnetic field formed by coils oriented parallel to a plane. The constricted nozzle acts as a nozzle flare, increasing the ratio of a plasma column's width to its length in the plane parallel to the magnetic field. In the experimental data discussed, the plasma column's 2:1 aspect ratio results from the superimposition of a solenoidal magnetic field and a quadrupole field produced by coils arranged at a 45-degree angle. For sufficiently large flare angles and gas pressures, the plasma column's axial inhomogeneity triggers instability, exhibiting characteristics similar to those of a z pinched mode. This phenomenon is quantified using mirror ratio curves, obtained by analyzing fluctuations in parameters such as ion saturation current and 2.5 MHz electromagnetic radiation measured using probe arrays. The findings suggest that the flared nozzle acts as a amplifier for global mirror instabilities, increasing their growth rates compared to a cylindrical plasma. However, our experiment demonstrates that a rotating droplet of superfluid 4He can exhibit viscoelastic behavior when subjected to an applied stress, showing both a viscosity-like term and a shear elastic response proportional to the strain.  This phenomenon arises from the dynamic rearrangement of the vortex lattice and the formation of "beaver plugs" in the droplet's boundary, which break off and enter the droplet under sufficient stress.  The creation of these beaver plugs significantly raises the droplet's internal viscosity and contributes to an elastic shear response due to the substantial resistance experienced by them as they move into the droplet, plausibly attributed to the formation of solid-like cores within the vortices.  The formation of these beaver plugs also results in plastic flow and a yielding stress point, which are attributes of viscoelastic behavior in fluids.  Furthermore, our research employs in-situ neutron imaging and an extensive range of applied stresses, thereby providing a comprehensive insight into the viscoelastic behavior of superfluids.  Moreover, our discovery that beaver plug creation is a general phenomenon in confined superfluids implies that vortex-line creations and removals may exhibit elastic and viscous characteristics, thereby potentially affecting the universal thermal conductivity of superfluids.  Lastly, our research also reveals that the formation of "beaver plugs" is also a general phenomenon in the creation of solid-like formations in mesoscopic superfluid droplets subject to rotational stirring.  Furthermore, our experiment shows that the formation and creation of these beaver plugs is also affected by friction between the droplet and the substrate as well as by thermal fluctuations which can start the vortex creation and removal processes.  In this experiment, a range of variables such as the droplet size, its boundary, the applied stresses, and temperatures were studied and confirmed to be influential in the formation of these beaver plugs and the creation of the plastic flow and yield points observed.  The research also shows that the formation of these beaver plugs is also affected by an applied thermal gradient when the droplet is placed on an heated stage as well as by an applied electrical current when the droplet is placed within a very weak magnetic field, thereby indicating that the formation of these beaver plugs is also influenced by friction and the stability of the vortex lattice. Traditionally, these observations have been analyzed by establishing a four-dimensional spatial metric from the CMB data, but we now propose to directly fit the CMB data into a gravitational wave metric. This wave metric is derived from the Liouville action and includes two constants: the gravitational field amplitude and the spin parity. By employing the 2018 Planck dataset and conducting statistical analyses, we have determined the estimated values of these CMB metric parameters, with the results consistent with those of standard inflationary theories, with an estimated $A \times 10^{15}$ ranging from 0.46 to 2.24, with 95% confidence, and the spin parity estimated at 0.79, with a range of -0.07 to 0.31, with 95% confidence. This CMB metric provides a unique window into the universe's initial state and could potentially be used in conjunction with gravitational wave data from binary mergers to make inferences about primordial gravitational waves. Furthermore, the CMB metric allows us to make predictions about the universe's large-scale structure and Sloan Digital Sky Survey data are consistent with the universe's initial state described by the gravitational wave metric. This CMB metric is also capable of being experimentally verified through future experiments like Billington experiment and Cosmic microwave B-pol, making it a physically significant concept. Overall, with future experiments, we may uncover CMB memory, providing insight into the universe's initial conditions and allowing us to distinguish between conventional cosmology and alternative theories of gravity. This CMB memory is also capable of being influenced by some alternative theories of gravity, with the predicted scales and amplitudes of the gravitational wave metric shown to be within the reach of experimental detection.

The incorporation of memristive properties into graphene, specifically in its single-layer form, has shown the potential to achieve resistive switching and variability stemming from multiple sources.  However, these effects are often difficult to control and are typically triggered by high-energy processes that alter the graphene's crystal structure.  To address these limitations, we investigated the effects of introducing defects at the edge sites of graphene's unit cells, where dopants such as H, F, and Cl, are incorporated.  The presence of these defects enables fine-tuned resistive switching and variability with lower energy activation.  The results of our research demonstrate that defect sites at graphene's edges offer a feasible path to achieving controlled, efficient, and stable resistive switching and variability essential for dynamic graphene-based devices.  The theoretical resistance changes of up to three orders of magnitude provide substantial storage capacity for graphene-based memory and neuroadaptive devices.  Additionally, we have identified potential pathways for thermal relaxation that could restore graphene's conductivity, even when it has undergone significant damage.  The research further suggests that incorporating additional atoms, such as Cl, may enhance graphene's conductance and increase its resilience to backpropagation and recall interference. Using a conforming finite element method with mesh-dependent parameters, we analyze the error of the approximate solution and demonstrate that it converges with a rate of O(ε^(-1/2)) when the mesh size tends to zero, albeit at a lower rate than that due to numerical differentiation, which is O(ε). The proposed method can also be extended to the case of a piecewise constant function φ, which is essential for the numerical analysis of a variety of physical phenomena. For instance, we considered the case of a chemical reaction on a thin film undergoing phase transitions due to a change in the surface energy, as well as a film undergoing spiking due to strong electrical properties and a delicate membrane protecting a cell from external stresses. for semi-supervised learning problems, they often fall short in enhancing labeling efforts for unlabeled data. This limitation stems from features extracted from semi-supervised unlabeled data and from labeled data, which inevitably differ and thus lead to separate clustering outcomes. Consequently, most existing unsupervised semi-supervised learning techniques are unable to accurately correct labeling errors. To address this issue, we suggest leveraging self-supervised learning to generate universal features that do not diverge from labeled data characteristics. By using these unified features, we can improve the accuracy of classification-based label correction methods and thereby improve the overall labeling efficiency in semi-supervised learning settings. Our proposed technique can function as a general enhancement method for various semi-supervised learning frameworks. Experimental results demonstrate that the feature unified using self-supervised learning yields better labeling accuracy compared to conventional methods which solely rely on classification or contrastive learning. For instance, when applied to MNIST and CIFAR10 datasets, our technique improves labeling accuracy by +1.3% and +4.2%, respectively, and outperforms supervised contrastive learning by +1.4% and +2.3% on the same datasets. The source code for our technique can be accessed via this link: https://github.com/darc027/SelfSup-Label-Correction, and we have made the pre-trained model for CIFAR10 available via this link: https://huggingface.co/DARC2022SelfSupLabelCorrection/. Our vision is to integrate self-supervised learning to develop more effective annotation methods that can leverage large amounts of unlabeled data to improve labeling efficiency. With significant labeling costs in many real-world applications such as autonomous driving, our research aims to enable cost-effective supervision settings that can achieve high labeling accuracy. This paper introduces an innovative method for rapidly computing environment maps in real-time based on a limited number of light sources. This method also preserves the standard render state and does not consume any additional graphics resources. This feature serves as a real-time equivalent to offline computed environment maps.
